'''Alastair Graham Walter Cameron''' (21 June 1925 &ndash; 3 October 2005)<ref name=":0">{{cite journal|title=Alastair G. W. Cameron, 80, Theorist on Creation of Moon, Dies|journal=NY Times|date=2005|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2005/10/29/science/space/29cameron.html}}</ref> was an American–Canadian [[astrophysicist]] and space scientist who was an eminent staff member of the [[Astronomy]] department of [[Harvard University]]. He was one of the founders of the field of [[nuclear astrophysics]], advanced the theory that the Moon was created by the [[Giant-impact hypothesis|giant impact]] of a Mars-sized object with the early Earth, and was an early adopter of computer technology in astrophysics.

== Early life and education ==
Alastair Cameron was born in [[Winnipeg]], Manitoba, to parents of Scottish descent. His father, born in [[London|London, England]], was chemist A.T. Cameron, a professor and chair of the biochemistry department at [[University of Manitoba|Manitoba Medical College]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite news|url=https://news.harvard.edu/gazette/story/2009/12/alastair-graham-walter-cameron/|title=Alastair Graham Walter Cameron|date=2009-12-17|work=Harvard Gazette|access-date=2018-10-31|language=en-US}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite news|url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/technology/alastair-cameron-astrophysicist-1925-2005/article25679035/|title=Alastair Cameron, Astrophysicist, 1925-2005|work=The Globe and Mail|access-date=2018-10-31}}</ref> He recalls addressing all men as “Doctor” as a four-year-old, noting it was "clearly an early attempt at forming a hypothesis based on limited data."<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal|last=Cameron|first=A. G. W.|date=1999|title=Adventures in Cosmogony|journal=Annual Review of Astronomy and Astrophysics|language=en|volume=37|issue=1|pages=1–36|doi=10.1146/annurev.astro.37.1.1|bibcode=1999ARA&A..37....1C|issn=0066-4146}}</ref>

In 1940 (When Cameron was only 15 years old), he made a bet with a high school classmate that man would land on the [[Moon]] within 40 years. When the [[Apollo program]] achieved a successful Moon landing in 1969, the former classmate sent a cheque to settle the bet, which Cameron had framed and hung on the wall in his office.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":1" />

Cameron earned a [[Bachelor of Science]] degree from the [[University of Manitoba]] in Physics and Mathematics. During the summers, he worked at the [[Chalk River Laboratories|Chalk River Laboratory]], a Canadian research facility on [[Ontario]].<ref name=":6">{{Cite journal|last=David|first=Arnett|date=2017|title=A. G. W. Cameron 1925-2005, Biographical Memoir|journal=National Academy of Sciences|arxiv=1708.05429 |language=en|bibcode=2017arXiv170805429A}}</ref> He went on to do graduate work in both theoretical and experimental nuclear physics at the [[University of Saskatchewan]]. Under the supervision of [[Leon Katz (physicist)|Leon Katz]], he studied [[Photodisintegration|photonuclear]] [[Nuclear cross section|cross sections]] using the university's new 25 [[Electronvolt|MeV]] [[betatron]] accelerator. In 1952, earned the first PhD awarded in physics from the university.<ref name=":3">{{cite journal|author=Wasserburg, Gerald J.|author-link=Gerald J. Wasserburg|title=Obituary: Alastair Graham Walter Cameron|journal=Physics Today|date=January 2006|volume=59|issue=1|pages=68–70|doi=10.1063/1.2180186|bibcode = 2006PhT....59a..68W |url=https://authors.library.caltech.edu/42547/1/1.2180186.pdf }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://library.usask.ca/archives/campus-history/honorary-degrees.php?id=348&view=detail|title=Honorary Degrees - University of Saskatchewan|website=library.usask.ca|language=en|access-date=2018-10-31}}</ref>

== Career ==
After finishing his PhD, he spent two years as an assistant professor at the [[Iowa State University|Iowa State College]] and worked at the [[Ames Laboratory]] at the university, which was run by the [[United States Atomic Energy Commission]]. There he taught nuclear physics and helped to increase the electron beam current in the facility's new 70-MeV [[synchrotron]] particle accelerator.<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":6" />

While at the Ames lab, he read an article in [[Science News|''Science News Letter'']] magazine (now ''Science News''), about the detection of the element [[technetium]] in the variable star [[R Andromedae]] and other red variable stars by the American astronomer [[Paul W. Merrill|Paul Merrill]]. Since this element has no stable isotopes, the observed technetium would experience radioactive decay with [[half-life]] of about 200,000 years, which was much shorter than the lifetime of the star. Cameron realized that this meant the technetium must have formed inside the stars where it was observed, by bombarding other elements with [[neutron]]s. Excited by this clue to the astrophysical origins of [[Heavy metals|heavy elements]], Cameron decided to switch fields study astrophysics.<ref name=":6" /><ref name=":2" /> Having never taken an astronomy class, he purchased several graduate-level textbooks, subscribed to ''[[the Astrophysical Journal]]'', and began an intense period of self-study.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":5" />

=== Stellar nucleosynthesis ===
Cameron returned to Canada in 1954, taking a position at the Chalk River Laboratory operated by [[Atomic Energy of Canada Limited]]. There he hoped to apply advances from the rapidly developing field of nuclear physics to the field of astrophysics. In particular, he wished to calculate the [[nuclear cross section]]s involved in [[Triple-alpha process|helium]] [[Nuclear fusion|fusion]] reactions inside the cores of [[Red giant|red giant stars]], which could produce the neutrons necessary to produce the technetium observed by Merrill.<ref name=":5" /> He quickly realized that traditional computational methods and [[slide rule]]s were insufficient to calculate complex networks of nuclear reactions. He used of some of the first computers in Canada, originally purchased for use by the accounting department at the laboratory, to do the calculations.<ref name=":2" /> At first, he was able to give programs on trays of punch cards to the accountants to run on his behalf. However, as his calculations increased in sophistication and the computing resources at Chalk River improved, he switched to work during the night and on weekends when the machines were not in use.<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":6" />

In 1957, he published ''[[bibcode:1957PASP...69..201C|Nuclear Reactions in Stars and Nucleogenesis]]'', known as the AGWC paper, which introduced an important, early, comprehensive theory of the production of [[chemical element]]s in [[star]]s, especially [[r-process]] elements. This work by Cameron, along with the [[B2FH paper|B<sup>2</sup>FH paper]] (published in the same year by  [[Margaret Burbidge]], [[Geoffrey Burbidge]], [[William Alfred Fowler|William A. Fowler]], and [[Fred Hoyle]]), helped to publicise and direct research in the field of [[nuclear astrophysics]].<ref name=":3" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://theconversation.com/elements-from-the-stars-the-unexpected-discovery-that-upended-astrophysics-66-years-ago-93916|title=Elements from the stars: The unexpected discovery that upended astrophysics 66 years ago|last1=Spyrou|first1=Artemis|last2=Schatz|first2=Hendrik|website=The Conversation|date=2 May 2018 |language=en|access-date=2019-10-26}}</ref>

In 1959, after growing frustrated with what he saw as the Canadian government's lack of interest in investing in science, Cameron emigrated to the United States, which had just seen a major expansion of  funding for space-science research due to the [[Sputnik crisis]].<ref name=":4">{{Cite news|url=https://www.aip.org/history-programs/niels-bohr-library/oral-histories/33763|title=Alastair Cameron|date=2015-01-12|work=American Institute of Physics, Niels Bohr Library & Archives, Oral History Interviews|access-date=2018-11-12|language=en}}</ref><ref name=":3" /> He held academic positions at the [[California Institute of Technology]], the [[Goddard Institute for Space Studies]], and at [[Yeshiva University]]. In 1973 he became a professor of astronomy at [[Harvard University]] and remained there for 26 years. From 1976 to 1982 he was chairman of the Space Science Board of the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]].

Five days before his death in 2005, the 2006 Bethe Prize for his work on nuclear astrophysics was announced. Cameron would receive this award for his 50-year-old work on stellar nucleosynthesis, which was still an area of active research.

=== Formation of the Solar System ===
After learning about the 1960 discovery of an excess of [[Isotopes of xenon|xenon-129]] due to the radioactive decay of [[iodine-129]] in the [[Richardton meteorite]], Cameron became interested in what the abundances of radioactive isotopes can tell us about the formation of the [[Formation and evolution of the Solar System|Solar System]] and the [[interstellar medium]]. In 1975, he gave a seminar at [[California Institute of Technology|Caltech]], titled ''The Origin of the Solar System'', where he outlined a unified model of the formation of the Solar System, from the Sun's formation from the collapse of cloud of gas and dust, the subsequent formation of a [[protoplanetary disk]], to the formation of the [[gas giant]]s and the [[terrestrial planet]]s out of material from the disk. When an audience member asked, “What did you do on the seventh day?” he reportedly responded, “I rested.”<ref name=":3" />

=== Formation of the Moon ===
Samples brought back from the [[Apollo program]] showed that the Moon was composed of the same material as the mantle of the Earth. This surprising result was still unexplained in the early 1970s, when Cameron began work on an explanation of the Moon's origins. He theorized that the formation of the Moon was the result of a tangential impact of an object at least the size of [[Mars]] on the early [[Earth]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.daviddarling.info/encyclopedia/C/Cameron.html|title=Cameron, Alastair G. W. (Graham Walter) (1925-2005)|last=Darling|first=David|website=www.daviddarling.info|access-date=2018-11-14}}</ref> In this model, the outer silicates of the body hitting the Earth would be vaporized, whereas a metallic core would not. The more volatile materials that were emitted during the collision would escape the Solar System, whereas silicates would tend to coalesce. Hence, most of the collisional material sent into orbit would consist of silicates, leaving the coalescing Moon deficient in iron and volatile materials, such as water.

After seeing [[William Kenneth Hartmann|William Hartmann]] present a similar, independent model at a conference in 1974, Cameron began a several decade-long collaboration with Hartmann to develop the [[giant-impact hypothesis]].<ref name=":0" /> Cameron was able to use increasingly sophisticated computer models to show that such a collision could produce an Earth-Moon system with the correct mass, spin, and orbital momentum.<ref name=":1" /> The giant-impact theory gained mainstream acceptance as the scientific explanation for the origin of the Moon beginning in the 1980s.<ref name=":0" />

After his retirement from Harvard in 1999, Cameron held a position at the [[Lunar and Planetary Laboratory]] of the [[University of Arizona]].<ref name=":1" />

== Personal life ==
Cameron married Elizabeth MacMillan in 1955.<ref name=":1" /> She died in 2001.<ref name=":0" />

While Cameron became a naturalized United States citizen in 1963 in order to receive the security clearances necessary to work in the US space program, he frequently returned to visit his native Canada and remained active in Canadian politics throughout his life.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://history.nasa.gov/biosa-d.html|title=Biographies of Aerospace Officials and Policymakers, A-D|website=history.nasa.gov|access-date=2018-11-14}}</ref><ref name=":2" />

Cameron died on October 3, 2005,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.spaceref.com/news/viewpr.html?pid=18092|title=Obituary: Alastair G.W. Cameron, Noted Astrophysicist and Space Scientist|date=October 21, 2005|website=SpaceRef|access-date=June 14, 2010|archive-date=May 27, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200527111728/http://www.spaceref.com/news/viewpr.html?pid=18092|url-status=dead}}</ref> from heart failure. He was 80 years old.
